deleted.text: Every flag is declared in the flags repository as one entry of the ruleset file.
An entry names the flag, its kind, its owner, its default value, its variants and its targeting rules.
A pull request to the ruleset needs approval from the flag's owner and from one platform engineer.
Names are lowercase words joined by dots and begin with the owning area, as in checkout.express-pay.
All flags are evaluated once per request by the edge gateway.
The gateway writes every result into the X-Flag-Snapshot header, and downstream services read flag values from that header only.
Services never call the flag store themselves.
The flag store pushes a new ruleset to the gateway within a few seconds of a merge to the flags repository.
The gateway evaluates every active flag for every request, which keeps the snapshot complete for whichever service reads it.
Targeting rules match on the user ID, the country and the client platform.
Percentage rollouts hash the user ID with the flag name, so a user stays in the same bucket as the percentage grows.
Because the snapshot is computed once at the edge, every service that handles a request sees the same value for a flag, even if the ruleset changes while the request is in flight.
A request that fans out to five services therefore never mixes two variants of one flag.
Merge the flag with its default set to off and no targeting rules.
Unit tests read flags through a small helper that parses the snapshot header, so a test sets the header on the fake request to choose a variant.
Integration tests run against a gateway stub that emits a fixed snapshot.
Every test suite covers both values of each release flag it touches.
If the gateway cannot reach the flag store, it keeps serving the last ruleset it received and raises an alert after five minutes.
If a request arrives at a service without a snapshot header, the helper treats every flag as its default value and logs a warning.
A release flag must be deleted by its remove_by date.
The weekly flag report lists flags past their date, and the owner deletes the flag and the dead code path in one pull request.
Experiment flags are deleted within two weeks of the end of the test.
Operational flags have no removal date and stay for as long as the feature they guard.
The owning team answers for a flag from creation to deletion.
When a team is dissolved, its flags pass to the team that inherits its code.
The platform team owns the flag store, the gateway evaluation and the helper library.
Whether the rollout log should move from the wiki into the ruleset entry.

candidates.sentence: The ruleset is a plain JSON document that anyone can read in review, not a compiled artifact that needs a build to change.
Flag names describe the behaviour a user sees rather than the ticket number under which the work was planned.
A flag name is never reused once the flag has been deleted, even years later.
Outside payments, a team may give a flag an on default when the old code path is the riskier of the two.
A flag value is worked out inside the service that uses it, not decided upstream and handed along with the request.
Evaluating a flag therefore costs no network hop, and no service waits on another component to learn which variant a user gets.
Our SDK keeps no evaluation results between requests, so a ruleset change reaches users on the very next refresh.
A flag with no targeting rules returns its declared default to every user.
They can disagree for up to 30 seconds after a ruleset change, while some instances still hold the previous ruleset.
A handler that must not see two values of one flag reads it once at the start and keeps that value until it returns.
Merge the flag with its default set to the old behaviour and no targeting rules.
No test has to build a flag snapshot header any more, since the fixture answers every question about a flag directly.
Integration tests start the SDK with a fixed ruleset file instead of the flag store.
If the SDK cannot reach the flag store, it keeps evaluating against the last ruleset it fetched and raises an alert after five minutes.
